content: The Surname Project A is a genetic genealogy initiative that employs genealogical DNA testing to trace male lineage. In many cultures, surnames are inherited from father to son, and similarly, Y-chromosomes (Y-DNA) are passed down from father to son with a predictable mutation rate. This allows individuals with the same surname to use DNA testing to determine whether they share a common ancestor within recent history. When two males share a surname, testing their Y-chromosome markers can reveal whether they are related or unrelated. If they are related, the number of markers tested and the degree of matches at those markers help estimate the number of generations back to their most recent common ancestor (MRCA). For instance, if two individuals match on 37 markers, there is a 50% probability that their MRCA lived less than five generations ago and a 90% probability that the MRCA lived less than 17 generations ago. Markers Y-DNA tests analyze between 10 and 67 markers on the Y chromosome. Most surname projects recommend testing at least 25 markers. The test results indicate the number of repeats a subject has at a specific marker, with these variations in repeats referred to as alleles. For example, at marker DYS455, the results might show 8, 9, 10, 11, or 12 repeats. The specific results for an individual are collectively referred to as a haplotype. When a surname project has a sufficient number of participants, it can identify one or more modal haplotypes associated with that surname. Testing Companies Surname projects are now hosted by various testing companies. These companies often offer group rates for surname projects, and some laboratories store submitted DNA samples for several years at no additional cost to participants. This storage allows for further testing as new technologies or methods become available. Haplogroups The Y chromosome has been extensively studied and categorized into Human Y-chromosome DNA haplogroups based on the number of alleles at specific positions, known as markers. These markers are selected for their proven ability to predict the haplogroup of the tested individual. The specific markers used are proprietary information and vary between testing companies, although there is significant overlap among them. This overlap has enabled Y-STR database websites, such as Ybase and Ysearch, to convert scores from different companies and identify matches within their databases for submitted results.
